Designing a Real-Time Load Bidding Platform (Uber Freight)

Simulate this design Draw it from memory

Difficulty: Advanced Topics: Real-Time Auction, WebSocket, Event-Driven, Concurrency, Sorted Sets Asked at: Uber Freight, Convoy, Loadsmart, Amazon Logistics, Flexport Prerequisites: Message Queues, WebSockets, Caching, and Distributed Locking

1. Understanding the Problem

A load bidding platform is a real-time auction marketplace for freight. Shippers post loads (cargo that needs to move from A to B), and carriers (truck owners) compete by placing bids – offering a price and pickup time. All bidders see new bids appear live without refreshing. When the auction closes (time expires or shipper accepts a bid), exactly one carrier wins and gets the booking. The challenge is handling concurrent bids at scale while maintaining real-time fan-out and ensuring exactly-one-winner semantics at auction close.💡 Fan-out = one event having to reach many recipients. Here a single bid must land on every screen watching that load, so the cost of a write is multiplied by the size of the audience.

2. Naive First Cut

How this breaks:

  • Every bid writes to Postgres and then all other carriers must poll to see new bids – 50K carriers watching 5-10 loads each is 500K watch relationships, and a 5-second poll on each is ~100K requests/sec
  • Determining the current best bid requires SELECT * FROM bids WHERE load_id=? ORDER BY price LIMIT 1 on every view – index contention at write scale💡 Index contention = reads and writes fighting over the same index pages. Every new bid has to update the index that every “who is winning?” query is simultaneously reading. Learn more →
  • When auction closes, two concurrent processes might both read the same “best bid” and create two bookings – double-award
  • Carriers watching a load see bids with 5-10 second delay (polling interval) – in a competitive auction, stale data means unfair bidding
  • No durability story – if the API server crashes between accepting a bid and writing to DB, the bid is lost permanently
  • Carrier places a bid, refreshes, doesn’t see it yet – confusing user experience (UX) due to replication lag💡 Replication lag = the delay before a copy of the database catches up with the original. If the refresh lands on a copy that is half a second behind, the carrier’s own bid is genuinely not there yet.

The rest of the doc evolves this into a production-grade auction system.

3. Prior Art We’re Drawing From

  • Uber Freight Carrier Marketplace – Scoring-based matching where carriers see available loads ranked by relevance. Loads can be “instant book” (first-come) or auction-style where the best bid wins. (Uber Freight Engineering)
  • Google Ad Exchange (AdX) – Real-time bidding at millisecond scale (100ms auction window). Uses in-memory bid aggregation and pub/sub for result delivery. The pattern of “collect bids in a time window, pick winner, notify all” is directly applicable to freight auctions. (Google Ad Manager Docs)
  • eBay Auction Architecture – Pioneered anti-sniping (extend auction if late bid arrives), bid history fan-out to watchers, and optimistic concurrency on bid placement. (eBay Tech Blog)💡 Optimistic concurrency = don’t lock anything; just check at write time that nobody changed the row underneath you, and retry if they did. Deep Dive 2 uses exactly this to stop two closers awarding one load.
  • Redis Sorted Sets for Leaderboards – Gaming platforms use ZADD/ZRANGE for real-time leaderboards at 100K+ updates/sec. Same pattern applies to bid ranking where score = price. (Redis Best Practices)
  • Kafka Event Sourcing for Financial Systems – Stripe and Square use Kafka as the source of truth for financial events, enabling replay and audit trails. Bid events have similar durability requirements – you need a complete audit trail of who bid what and when.💡 Event sourcing = store the ordered list of things that happened, and treat every table as a view you can rebuild by replaying it. It is why a lost Redis leaderboard here is an inconvenience rather than a data loss.

4. Functional Requirements

Core (Top 3)

  1. Shipper posts a load for auction – origin, destination, weight, max budget, auction duration. Eligible carriers are notified.
  2. Carriers place bids in real-time – bid a price and estimated pickup time. All watchers see new bids appear live (< 500ms latency).
  3. Auction closes and winner is determined – when time expires or shipper accepts a bid, exactly one carrier wins. Booking is created atomically.

Below the Line

  • Carrier can withdraw a bid before auction closes
  • Shipper can set a “buy now” price that instantly awards the load
  • Anti-sniping: extend auction if bid arrives in last 2 minutes
  • Bid history and audit trail
  • Carrier reputation scoring factors into bid ranking
  • Auto-bidding rules (carrier pre-sets: “bid X on any Delhi-Mumbai load under Y price”)

5. Non-Functional Requirements

Core

NFR (non-functional requirement) Target
Bid-to-display latency < 500ms from bid placed to all watchers seeing it
Auction close consistency Exactly one winner – no double-award under any failure
Bid durability Zero bid loss even on service crash (financial audit requirement)
Concurrent bidders 500 bids/sec total, up to 200 carriers watching a single hot load
Availability 99.9% – carriers can always place bids
scroll →

Below the Line

  • 20K concurrent open auctions
  • 50K connected carriers via WebSocket
  • Bid placement < 200ms response time (acknowledgment)
  • Auction results delivered within 5 seconds of close

6. Scale Estimation (Back-of-Envelope)

  • Open auctions: 20K at any time
  • Bid rate: 500 bids/sec peak (across all auctions)
  • Hot auction: Popular route gets 100+ bids in 15 minutes (~0.1 bids/sec per load)
  • WebSocket connections: 50K carriers, each watching 5-10 loads = up to 500K subscriptions
  • Storage: Bids are small (~200 bytes each). 500/sec x 86400 = 43M bids/day x 200B = ~8.6GB/day

7. Core Entities

  • Shipper – posts loads, sets auction parameters, accepts bids or lets timer decide.
  • Carrier – bids on loads, has rating, truck capacity, region preferences.
  • Load – cargo to move. Has origin, destination, weight, auction window, status.
  • Bid – carrier’s offer on a load. Price, estimated pickup time, composite score, status.
  • Auction – lifecycle wrapper around a load’s bidding period. Start time, end time, current state.
  • Booking – created when auction closes. Links winning carrier to load. Triggers payment flow.

8. API / System Interface

💡 Every endpoint below is authenticated with a JWT (JSON Web Token) — a signed blob the client sends on each request that proves who it is. The signature is what lets the server trust the caller’s identity without a database lookup, and it is why the server never takes the bidder’s identity from the request body. Learn more →

POST /api/v1/loads
  Body: { shipperId, originLat, originLng, destLat, destLng, weightTons, goodsType, maxPrice, auctionDurationMin }
  Response: { loadId, auctionEndsAt, status: "OPEN" }
  Auth: JWT Bearer (shipper)
  Note: Idempotent via X-Idempotency-Key header.

POST /api/v1/loads/{loadId}/bids
  Body: { carrierId, price, estimatedPickupTime }
  Response: { bidId, rank, currentBestPrice, status: "ACCEPTED" }
  Auth: JWT Bearer (carrier)
  Note: Validates auction is still open, price > 0, carrier is eligible.

DELETE /api/v1/loads/{loadId}/bids/{bidId}
  Response: { status: "WITHDRAWN" }
  Auth: JWT Bearer (carrier -- must own this bid)

POST /api/v1/loads/{loadId}/accept
  Body: { bidId }
  Response: { bookingId, winnerCarrierId, price }
  Auth: JWT Bearer (shipper -- must own this load)
  Note: Early acceptance -- closes auction immediately.

GET /api/v1/loads/{loadId}/bids
  Response: { bids: [{bidId, carrierId, price, rank, placedAt}], bestPrice, bidCount, auctionEndsAt }
  Auth: JWT Bearer (shipper or participating carrier)

WebSocket /ws/v1/loads/{loadId}/live
  Server pushes: { type: "NEW_BID", bidId, price, rank, bidCount }
  Server pushes: { type: "AUCTION_CLOSED", winnerId, winnerPrice }
  Auth: JWT ticket in connection params
  Note: the contract the < 500ms requirement needs. The high-level design starts
        with polling against GET /bids and Deep Dive 3 earns this endpoint.

9. High-Level Design

FR1: Shipper Posts a Load for Auction

Components introduced:

  • Load Service – CRUD (create, read, update, delete) for loads, triggers auction creation
  • Notification Service – alerts eligible carriers about new loads
  • Postgres – source of truth for loads and auction metadata

New components:

  • API Gateway: The single front door every app request passes through. It checks the caller’s token, applies rate limits, and routes to whichever service owns the path, so none of the services behind it has to re-implement authentication. Learn more →
  • Kafka: load-events: A durable, append-only log of “a load was posted / cancelled / awarded”. The Load Service writes to it and walks away; the Notification Service reads at its own pace. It exists so that a slow or dead notifier cannot slow down or fail a shipper’s post.

Flow:

  1. Shipper calls POST /loads with cargo details and auction duration
  2. Load Service validates, inserts load into Postgres with status=OPEN, auction_end = now + duration
  3. Publishes LOAD_POSTED event to Kafka topic load-events
  4. Notification Service consumes event, finds eligible carriers (geo + capacity match), sends push notifications
  5. Carriers open the load page and start watching the bid board

What FR1 leaves broken: a load now exists and carriers know about it, but nothing is an auction yet. Nothing is counting down to auction_end and nothing will act when it passes – FR3 builds that. Separately, Notification Service does a geo-plus-capacity scan across all 50K carriers on every post; at 20K open auctions that scan is the slowest thing in this path, and this design does not fix it.

FR2: Carriers Place Bids (the hot path)

New components:

  • Bid Service – validates a bid, writes it, and reads back its rank
  • bids table in Postgres – every bid for every load, with a composite score

Build the obvious thing first: a bid is a row, and the leaderboard is a sort over those rows.

Flow:

  1. Carrier calls POST /loads/{loadId}/bids with price and estimated pickup time
  2. Bid Service validates: auction still open? carrier eligible? price above the shipper’s floor?
  3. Computes the composite score – price weighted against carrier rating and pickup time
  4. INSERT INTO bids (load_id, carrier_id, price, score, placed_at) – synchronous, inside the carrier’s request
  5. Reads the rank back: SELECT count(*) FROM bids WHERE load_id=? AND score < ?
  6. Returns {bidId, rank, currentBestPrice} once both statements have committed
  7. Every other carrier watching this load has the page polling GET /loads/{loadId}/bids every 2 seconds
  8. That endpoint runs SELECT ... WHERE load_id=? ORDER BY score LIMIT 50 and returns the board as it stands

What FR2 leaves broken: three things, and only the first is obvious.

  • The 500ms target is simply not met. A 2-second poll means average staleness of one second and worst case two. Deep Dive 3 is where live push gets earned.
  • The poll volume is the real bill. 500K watch relationships at a 2-second interval is ~250K requests/sec, each one a sort, overwhelmingly to tell a carrier that nothing changed – 500 bids/sec spread over 20K open auctions is about one bid per auction every 40 seconds, so roughly 19 of every 20 polls return a board identical to the previous one.
  • One store is carrying both the hot path and the system of record. The same Postgres holds loads, bookings and the audit history, so a bid spike on a few hot lanes degrades auction close. And there is no ordered log of bid events, which means a dispute can only be answered from the current state of a mutable table. Deep Dive 1 takes the write path.💡 A hot lane is a popular route whose auctions draw far more bids than average. Traffic in this system is never spread evenly, so the few busiest loads set the load on everything sharing that database.

FR3: Auction Closes and Winner Determined

New components:

  • Auction Closer – cron job that finds expired auctions and awards them💡 A cron job is code run on a fixed timer. The timer is the catch: the auction ends at a precise instant, but a closer that wakes every 10 seconds only notices some time afterwards.
  • Booking Service – creates the final booking with ACID guarantees💡 ACID is the promise that a group of database writes either all land or none do, and that concurrent writers cannot see each other half-finished. That is what makes “flip the load to awarded and insert the booking” one indivisible step.

Flow:

  1. Auction Closer cron runs every 10 seconds
  2. Queries Postgres: SELECT load_id FROM loads WHERE status='OPEN' AND auction_end < NOW()
  3. For each expired auction: SELECT bid_id, carrier_id FROM bids WHERE load_id=? ORDER BY score LIMIT 1
  4. If no bids exist: mark load as EXPIRED, notify shipper
  5. If bids exist: begin Postgres transaction
  6. UPDATE loads SET status='AWARDED', winner_carrier_id=?, winner_bid_id=?
  7. INSERT INTO bookings (load_id, carrier_id, bid_id, price, status) VALUES (...)
  8. Commit transaction
  9. Publish LOAD_AWARDED event to Kafka
  10. Notification Service: notify winner (“You won!”) + notify losers (“Auction closed”)
  11. Watchers find out on their next poll – GET /loads/{id}/bids now returns status=AWARDED with the winner

What FR3 leaves broken: the closer is one process running an unguarded UPDATE. Run a single instance and it is a single point of failure sitting on the only step that produces revenue; run two for availability and both will see the same expired load and both will create a booking. Deep Dive 2 settles that. The 10-second tick is a second, quieter miss: the NFR asks for results within 5 seconds of close, and a tick-based closer averages 5 seconds of lag before it starts working, so it clears the bar roughly half the time.

scroll →

Why Redis Sorted Set for bid ranking, not Postgres ORDER BY? At 500 bids/sec with carriers constantly querying “what’s the current best bid” and “what’s my rank,” Postgres would be doing constant index scans on a hot table. Redis Sorted Set gives: ZADD O(log N) for new bids, ZRANGE 0 0 O(1) for best bid, ZRANK O(log N) for carrier’s position. All in-memory, sub-millisecond. We still persist to Postgres via Kafka for durability – Redis is the hot read layer.💡 A Redis Sorted Set is a collection where every member carries a numeric score and Redis keeps them in score order for you. That is a leaderboard as a built-in data structure, which is why “who is winning” stops being a query.

Why Kafka between Bid Service and Redis? Bid placement is financially significant – losing a bid is unacceptable. If Bid Service writes directly to Redis and Redis crashes, bids vanish. Kafka guarantees: once published, the bid is durable (replicated to 3 brokers). Consumer rebuilds Redis from Kafka on failure. Also provides a complete audit trail required for dispute resolution.

Why WebSocket over Server-Sent Events (SSE)? Carriers both receive updates (new bids from others) AND send actions (place their own bid). WebSocket is full-duplex – single connection handles both. SSE is one-directional (server-to-client only), requiring a separate HTTP endpoint for bid submission. WebSocket consolidates both into one connection, reducing overhead.💡 Full-duplex = both ends can send whenever they like on the same open connection, unlike ordinary HTTP where the client must ask before the server may answer.

11. Data Modeling

Redis Sorted Set (Bid Leaderboard – per load):

Key: "bids:{loadId}" -> Sorted Set
  Member: "{carrierId}:{bidId}"
  Score: composite_score (lower is better)
    Simple: score = price
    Advanced: score = 0.7*price + 0.2*distance_penalty + 0.1*(1/carrier_rating)

Key: "auction:{loadId}" -> Hash
  { status, endsAt, bidCount, bestPrice, bestCarrierId, shipperId }
  TTL: none (cleaned up by Auction Closer after completion)

Key: "carrier:bids:{carrierId}" -> Set
  Members: [loadId1, loadId2, ...]  (loads this carrier has active bids on)

Postgres (Auction DB):

CREATE TABLE loads (
    load_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    shipper_id UUID NOT NULL,
    origin_lat DECIMAL(10,7),
    origin_lng DECIMAL(10,7),
    dest_lat DECIMAL(10,7),
    dest_lng DECIMAL(10,7),
    weight_tons DECIMAL(6,2),
    goods_type VARCHAR(50),
    max_price DECIMAL(10,2),
    auction_start TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    auction_end TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,  -- OPEN, BIDDING, AWARDED, EXPIRED, CANCELLED
    winner_carrier_id UUID,
    winner_bid_id UUID,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);
CREATE INDEX idx_loads_status ON loads(status, auction_end);
CREATE INDEX idx_loads_shipper ON loads(shipper_id, created_at DESC);

CREATE TABLE bids (
    bid_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    load_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES loads(load_id),
    carrier_id UUID NOT NULL,
    price DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL,
    estimated_pickup_time TIMESTAMP,
    status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,  -- ACTIVE, OUTBID, WON, LOST, WITHDRAWN
    placed_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    composite_score DECIMAL(10,4)
);
CREATE INDEX idx_bids_load ON bids(load_id, composite_score ASC);
CREATE INDEX idx_bids_carrier ON bids(carrier_id, placed_at DESC);

CREATE TABLE bookings (
    booking_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    load_id UUID NOT NULL UNIQUE,  -- one booking per load
    carrier_id UUID NOT NULL,
    bid_id UUID NOT NULL,
    price DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL,
    status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,  -- CONFIRMED, CANCELLED, COMPLETED
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);
SQL

Kafka Topics:

Topic: bid-events (partitioned by loadId -- ordering preserved per auction)
  Key: loadId
  Value: { bidId, loadId, carrierId, price, estimatedPickup, timestamp, eventType }
  EventTypes: BID_PLACED, BID_WITHDRAWN, AUCTION_CLOSED, WINNER_DETERMINED
  Retention: 30 days (audit trail)

Topic: load-events (partitioned by loadId)
  Key: loadId
  Value: { loadId, eventType, shipperId, details, timestamp }
  EventTypes: LOAD_POSTED, AUCTION_EXTENDED, LOAD_CANCELLED, LOAD_AWARDED
  Retention: 30 days

Access Patterns:

Query Data Source How
Place a bid Kafka (write) + Redis (read after consume) Publish to Kafka, consumer does ZADD bids:{loadId}
Get current best bid Redis ZRANGE bids:{loadId} 0 0 WITHSCORES
Get my rank Redis ZRANK bids:{loadId} "{carrierId}:{bidId}"
Get all bids for a load Redis (hot) or Postgres (historical) ZRANGE bids:{loadId} 0 -1 WITHSCORES
Close auction and pick winner Redis + Postgres Read best from Redis, write booking in Postgres (ACID)
Live bid updates Redis Pub/Sub Subscribe to channel live:load:{loadId}
Carrier’s active bids Redis Set SMEMBERS carrier:bids:{carrierId}
Audit trail Kafka + Postgres Replay Kafka topic or query bids table

12. Deep Dives

Deep Dive 1: How do we rank 500 bids a second without losing one?

Bad: the design FR2 built – a row in Postgres, and the leaderboard is a sort over those rows.

  • Ranking is ORDER BY score LIMIT 50, and it runs on every one of the ~250K polls/sec from FR2. Postgres will index-scan it happily, but you are paying 250K index scans a second to answer a question whose answer changes about 12 times a second across the entire platform.
  • The same Postgres holds loads, bookings and history, so bid traffic on a few hot lanes competes directly with auction close and booking creation. One store is carrying the hot path and the system of record.
  • There is no ordered log. “I bid 1,850 at 14:02:03 and was not shown as the winner” can only be answered from the current contents of a mutable table.

the design FR2 built – a row in Postgres, and the leaderboard is a sort over those rows.

keep the Postgres write for durability, add a Redis Sorted Set for the ranking.

Bid Service publishes to Kafka and returns. One consumer owns both writes.

there is now a 100-200ms gap between the “bid accepted” response and the bid appearing in the leaderboard (consumer lag). The carrier sees a brief “processing” state. That is fine for freight and would not be for a stock exchange. If it grates: optimistic client-side update – render the bid locally on ack, reconcile when the server echoes it back.

Deep Dive 2: What stops two closer instances from awarding the same load twice?

Bad: the closer FR3 built – a 10-second cron running an UPDATE with no condition on it.

  • 20K auctions open at any moment on a 15-minute window means about 22 close every second, so roughly 220 expired loads land in each 10-second tick. Run a second instance for availability and both see the same 220 rows, both read the same best bid, and both insert a booking.
  • Two carriers are each told they won the same load. There is no clean recovery from that: by the time anyone notices, one of them has routed a truck.
  • Running a single instance is not the fix. It fails over, and during the gap expired auctions sit unawarded, which blows the “results within 5 seconds of close” target far harder than the tick already does.

the closer FR3 built – a 10-second cron running an with no condition on it.

take an explicit row lock – .

make the status transition itself the lock, with a conditional update.

Deep Dive 3: How does a bid reach 500K watching screens in under 500ms?

Bad: polling, the way FR2 built it.

  • 50K carriers each watching 5-10 loads is up to 500K watch relationships. At a 2-second interval that is ~250K requests/sec, and the NFR is still missed – average staleness one second, worst case two.
  • The waste is the interesting part. 500 bids/sec across 20K open auctions means a typical load changes about once every 40 seconds, so roughly 19 of every 20 polls return a board identical to the previous one.
  • Tightening the interval to 400ms to chase the NFR takes the request count to ~1.25M/sec and pushes the identical-response share to about 99%. You are paying five times as much to be wrong slightly less often.

polling, the way FR2 built it.

one WebSocket server. Carriers connect to it and the Bid Processor pushes.

N WebSocket instances, Redis Pub/Sub, one channel per load.

Deep Dive 4: If the winner is always whoever bids last, why would anyone bid early?

Bad: the fixed auction_end that FR3 closes on.

  • A carrier bids at T-1s. Deep Dive 3 pushes it to every watcher in well under 500ms, so they genuinely see it – and then the auction closes before anyone can type a number. The last bidder wins by arriving last, not by bidding best.
  • The second-order effect is what actually kills the marketplace. Carriers learn that bidding early only reveals their price to a sniper, so they stop bidding early. Boards sit empty for fourteen minutes and the shipper gets no price discovery at all, until one bid lands in the final seconds at maxPrice minus a rupee. The auction stops being an auction.

the fixed that FR3 closes on.

Fixed extension: if a bid arrives within the last 2 minutes, extend auction by 2 minutes.

Good + bid floor + carrier commitment deposit.

13. Design Self-Audit

Potential weakness Assessment
Stale reads after bid placement? Carrier sees “accepted” immediately. Leaderboard updates in 100-200ms. Acceptable – show “processing” indicator briefly.
Single point of failure? Redis: cluster with replicas. Kafka: 3 brokers, replication factor 2. Auction Closer: runs on 2+ instances but only one processes each loadId (Kafka partition guarantee).
Dead-letter for failed bids? Kafka consumer retries 3x. On persistent failure: send to a dead-letter queue (DLQ) topic. Alert ops. Carrier is notified “bid processing failed – please retry.”
Data freshness between Redis and Postgres? Redis is the hot layer (leaderboard). Postgres is cold (audit/history). Bid Processor writes both. On Redis crash: rebuild from Kafka. Postgres is always eventually consistent (< 5s lag).
Cost at scale? Redis: 20K sorted sets x ~22 bids avg x 100 bytes = ~45MB. Trivial. Kafka: 500 msg/sec x 200 bytes x 30 days retention = ~250GB. Moderate.
What if Kafka consumer lags? Bids pile up, leaderboard becomes stale. Monitor consumer lag. Scale consumers horizontally (more partitions). Alert if lag > 2 seconds. See backpressure for the general shape of this problem.

15. Final Architecture

New components:

  • Bid Processor: The single consumer that reads the bid-events partition for a load, computes the score, and writes both Redis and Postgres. It exists so there is exactly one writer per auction applying bids in one order — which is what removed the dual-write race in Deep Dive 1.
  • WebSocket Service: Holds the long-lived connections to carrier apps and pushes bid updates down them. It is a separate tier from the Bid Service because connections are long-lived state and bid handling is stateless request work; mixing them means you cannot scale either one independently.
  • Redis Pub/Sub: The internal broadcast channel between the Bid Processor and the WebSocket instances, one channel per load (live:load:{loadId}). It exists because the processor has no idea which of the ten WebSocket instances holds which carrier’s connection, and per-load channels keep that ignorance cheap.
  • Redis Sorted Sets + Cache: The live leaderboard for every open auction, plus cached auction and carrier metadata. It is a derived view, rebuildable from Kafka, which is why keeping it in memory is an acceptable risk.
